chapter_theme: Renown, earned above all through giving, is the one gain that outlasts the body. The chapter treats a life without it as a disgrace and a burden on the earth, indeed as no life at all.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of fame (231-233), the elevation of those who have it (234-235), the lowness of those who lack it (236-239), and both together (240).

231.reading: Give, and live so that renown arises: there is no other profit for a living being.
231.nuance: ஊதியம is a word for profit, so the verse puts its ethics in the language of a balance sheet. Parimelazhagar notes that learning and valour can also win fame, and that giving is named as the highest route to it.

232.reading: All that speakers have to say amounts to praise resting on those who give something to those who ask.
232.nuance: Parimelazhagar extends speech to poets' song, and he dismisses a reading that lets others have praise too ('say what you will, fame stays with the giver'), because it misses fame's excellence. The verse's sweep ('all that speakers say') is a large claim, even as hyperbole.

233.reading: Apart from towering, unmatched renown, there is nothing in the world that stands undying.
233.nuance: The verse doesn't say what makes fame unmatched. Parimelazhagar specifies gifts that are hardest to give, of life, limb and property, which raises the bar far above ordinary repute.

234.reading: If someone achieves far-reaching renown within the earth's bounds, the world of the gods doesn't honour the புலவர்.
234.nuance: The verse is elliptical: it doesn't say whom heaven honours in their place, and everything hinges on the identity of புலவர். I'm not confident any reading here is the verse's own. Parimelazhagar cites Purananuru 27 for the idea that the famous gain both worlds.

positions.position: புலவர் are sages who have reached that world, and it prefers the famous to them.
positions.quote: புத்தேள் உலகம் அவனையல்லது தன்னை எய்தி நின்ற ஞானிகளைப் பேணாது.

positions.position: புலவர் are the gods themselves, so named because they have wisdom.
புலவர் are the learned and the world is a future one: it will not honour intellect alone over the selfless and famous.

235.reading: A ruin that is really growth and a death that is really existence are hard to come by except for the skilled.
235.nuance: வித்தகர் praises skill, not goodness: for Parimelazhagar, the art of turning what doesn't last into what does. The reading depends on his derivation of நத்தம் from நந்து, growth, and on taking போல் as a filler, so its foundation is a philological argument.

positions.position: It is a doctrine of two bodies: the elemental body grows poor and dies while the body of fame grows rich and stands.
positions.quote: ஆக்கமாகும் கேடாவது, புகழ் உடம்பு செல்வம் எய்தப் பூத உடம்பு நல்கூர்தல்.

positions.position: It speaks of strength of character that grows fame amid hardship and establishes it even in dying, with no second body.
positions.quote: துன்பங்களுக்கிடையேகூட அவற்றைத் தாங்கும் வலிமையால் தமது புகழை வளர்த்துக் கொள்வதும்,

236.reading: If you appear, appear with renown; for those without it, not appearing is better than appearing.
236.nuance: Taken as birth, a command about how to be born can't be obeyed. Each commentator has to resolve that oddity, and how they do it shapes their positions.

positions.position: It means being born human, and for those lacking the qualities that lead to fame, an animal birth is better, since no one reviles animals.
positions.quote: அக்குணம் இல்லாதார் மக்களாய்ப் பிறத்தலின் விலங்காய்ப் பிறத்தல் நன்று.

positions.position: It means plainly that not being born is better.
தோன்று means entering a field of activity: excel there, or stay out of it.
positions.quote: எந்தத் துறையில் ஈடுபட்டாலும் அதில் புகழுடன் விளங்கவேண்டும்;

237.reading: Those who cannot live with renown: why do they resent the people who scorn them, instead of resenting themselves?
237.nuance: The scorn is accepted as a fair verdict. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is that a good name was within reach, so the failure is one's own.

238.reading: They say it is a disgrace for everyone in the world not to obtain the legacy called renown.
238.nuance: எச்சம் is what remains after one dies, and it also means offspring, which Pope's 'childless' seizes on. Manakkudavar and Parimelazhagar make a severe point: the lack of fame needs no other fault to justify disgrace.

239.reading: Land that bears a body without renown will decline in its blameless rich yield.
239.nuance: யாக்கை, 'body', is pointed: for Parimelazhagar, what lacks renown is merely a body, a load the land must carry. Moral failure has an effect on the soil here, which Kalaignar weakens to how the land is regarded.

240.reading: Those who live free of blame are the ones who live; those who live free of renown are the ones who don't.
240.nuance: The balanced form leaves no neutral ground, and Parimelazhagar states it outright: to lack blame is to have renown and to lack renown is to have blame. A quiet, harmless, obscure life has no place in this verse.

links.note: 233 names renown as the one thing in the world that doesn't die. 331 calls taking what doesn't last for what lasts the lowest kind of knowledge. Chapter 34 never excepts fame, so fame's permanence is exactly what the later chapter puts in doubt.
222 calls giving good even with no reward in any world. 231 calls giving, with renown, the sole profit of a life. The same act is valued for itself in one and as a gain in the other.
Both rest on எச்சம், what is left behind. 114 reads a person's worth from what remains after them, and 238 makes renown the remainder that everyone should leave.
The earth is morally responsive in both: it yields less under a body without fame, and laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty. Land is more than a backdrop to human conduct in the Kural.
The same reclassification of the living as dead, with different tests: renown in 240, knowing what is due in 214. The chapters on benevolence and fame are linked as cause and result.

source_issues: 231, 232, 235: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.

234: Parimelazhagar's gloss has the misprint புதல்வரைப் for புலவரைப். Kalaignar's entry also ends with stray editorial text praising the interpretation (இவற்றுள் ஈற்றில் ...), which isn't commentary and wasn't used.
